name: Ahimelek (priest)
title: The high priest of Nob who helped David
summary: Akimelech, from Eli's priestly line and son of Ahitub, was high priest in Nob – the priestly city that housed the tabernacle after Shiloh was destroyed. When David appeared as a fugitive claiming to be on a secret royal mission, Akimelech acted in good faith: he let David eat the holy bread of the Presence and handed over Goliath's sword from the sanctuary. The Edomite Doeg, who witnessed the event, reported it to Saul. The king interpreted Akimelech's help as treason, and despite the priest's defense – that he knew nothing of the conflict between David and the king – Saul ordered his execution along with that of 85 other priests. When the king's own soldiers refused to raise their hands against the Lord's anointed, Doeg took on the task. Only Akimelech's son Abiathar survived and fled to David. The tragedy in Nob became a symbol of Saul's escalating tyranny and abuse of power, and the incident with the bread gained lasting theological significance when Jesus later used it to emphasize that mercy outweighs ceremonial rules.
roles: keeper of the tabernacle at Nob

keyEvents.title: Gives David holy bread
keyEvents.description: When David fled from Saul and arrived at Nob, he claimed to Ahimelek that he was on a secret mission for the king. In good faith, Ahimelek gave him the showbread from the sanctuary, since no other bread was available.

keyEvents.title: Gives David Goliath's sword
keyEvents.description: Ahimelek also gave David the sword of the Philistine Goliath, which had been kept in the sanctuary wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod.

keyEvents.title: Doeg reports to Saul
keyEvents.description: The Edomite Doeg, who was present when David came to Nob, reported the incident to King Saul and accused Ahimelek of helping David's escape.

keyEvents.title: Defending Himself Before Saul
keyEvents.description: When Ahimelech was summoned before Saul, he defended himself by pointing out that he was unaware of the conflict between David and the king, and that David was a faithful and highly trusted servant in the king's house.

keyEvents.title: The Massacre at Nob
keyEvents.description: Saul ordered the execution of Ahimelech and all the priests in Nob. When Saul's own men refused to lay hands on the Lord's priests, Doeg carried out the massacre, killing 85 priests who wore the ephod.

keyEvents.title: Jesus Refers to the Event
keyEvents.description: Jesus used the incident with the showbread as an example when he defended his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, showing that mercy can override ceremonial laws. In the Gospel of Mark, Abiathar is mentioned as high priest, which has been the subject of much textual criticism.

versions.summary: Ahimelech was the high priest in Nob who unknowingly helped David when he fled from King Saul. He gave David holy bread and Goliath's sword, leading Saul to order a massacre of the priests in Nob. Ahimelech and 85 other priests were killed by Doeg the Edomite.
versions.title: The High Priest Who Helped David
versions.reason: [minor] The title is good and descriptive. One could consider specifying 'in Nob', but this is a stylistic choice and not an error.; [major] Ahimelech was not only a priest, but the high priest. His role should reflect this, as he was the leader of the priesthood in Nob.; [minor] The name is spelled inconsistently: 'Ahimelech' is used in the title and elsewhere, but 'Ahimelek' (without h) is used in the summary. It should be consistent.; [major] In Mark 2:26 Jesus mentions 'Abiathar' as the high priest, not Ahimelech. This is a well-known textual-critical and theological issue. The description should reflect this nuance, since Jesus actually names Abiathar in the Gospel of Mark, even though it was Ahimelech who gave the bread according to 1 Samuel.; [minor] Father ID 'Ahitub' is correct (Ahitub). Verified from 1 Sam 22:9.; [minor] Ebjatar/Abiathar as son is correct (1 Sam 22:20). ID 'ebjatar' is acceptable.

versions.summary: Ahimelech, son of Ahitub, served as high priest in the priestly town of Nob where the tabernacle was located after Shiloh fell. When David came to him as a fugitive from Saul, Ahimelech gave him the holy bread of the Presence and Goliath's sword in good faith – unaware that David was out of favor with the king. This act had fatal consequences: Doeg the Edomite accused Ahimelech before Saul, who interpreted the help as treason and ordered his execution along with 85 other priests. Only his son Abiathar escaped and fled to David. Ahimelech's fate illustrates both Saul's growing tyranny and the tragic consequences of abuse of power. The incident with the bread was later cited by Jesus as an example that mercy and human need outweigh ceremonial regulations.

footnotes.text: The name Ahimelech (Hebrew: אֲחִימֶלֶךְ, Ahimelekh) means 'my brother is king' or 'the brother is king'. The prefix 'ahi' means 'brother' and 'melekh' means 'king'. The name can be understood as a theophoric name where 'melekh' refers to God as king, thus 'my (divine) brother is the king'.

Nob was a priestly city that likely lay near Jerusalem, possibly on the Mount of Scopus or another high ground northeast of the city. It served as a temporary seat for the tabernacle after the destruction of Shiloh. Archaeological investigations have attempted to locate the city, but its exact location remains debated. Isaiah 10:32 mentions Nob as a place from which Jerusalem could be seen.

The showbread (Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים, lechem hapanim – 'bread of the presence') were twelve loaves placed on a special table in the sanctuary every Sabbath. Only priests were allowed to eat them (Lev 24:5–9). The fact that Ahimelech gave these to David became an important example in rabbinic and Christian tradition that human need can override ceremonial laws.

In Mark 2:26, Jesus refers to the incident with the showbread but mentions 'Abiathar' as high priest instead of Ahimelech. This has been the subject of much discussion. Some explanations include that Abiathar may have been more well-known, that the phrase 'in the days of Abiathar' refers to a broader time period, or that an early copyist error may exist. Some rabbinic sources suggest that father and son may have had overlapping priestly service.

Doeg the Edomite is described as Saul's 'chief shepherd' (1 Sam 21:8). The fact that an Edomite held a prominent position at the Israelite court is remarkable and reflects the complex political conditions during Saul's reign. Rabbinic tradition in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 106b) portrays Doeg as an example of a learned man who used his knowledge for evil.

The massacre of the 85 priests in Nob is one of the most dramatic events of Saul's reign and marks a turning point that illustrates the king's moral decline. The number of 85 priests who wore the ephod (linen garment) suggests that Nob housed a significant priestly community. Psalm 52, according to its superscription, is linked to Doeg's betrayal.

Ahimelech belonged to the priestly line of Eli, as he was the grandson of Phinehas and the great-grandson of Eli (cf. 1 Sam 14:3; 22:9,20). The massacre at Nob can therefore be seen as a partial fulfillment of the prophecy against the house of Eli in 1 Sam 2:31–36, where it was foretold that Eli's descendants would be struck by disaster.
